name: Toll Brothers, Inc.

profile.description: Toll Brothers, Inc. is the largest luxury homebuilder in the United States, building single-family detached and attached homes, active-adult communities, and rental apartments (Toll Brothers Apartment Living) in 24 states. Founded in 1967, the company targets roughly $10.5 billion in FY2026 home sales revenue from 471 selling communities. Karl Mistry, who joined in 2004 through the executive training program, succeeded Doug Yearley as CEO on March 30, 2026, and Yearley stayed on as Executive Chairman.

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Toll has grown beyond suburban luxury single-family homes into City Living, active-adult, and Apartment Living rentals. These are extensions of the same land-and-build model, not a business transformation [1][4]. AI Deployment (0/2): Our searches found no AI-powered customer products or quantified AI efficiency savings [3]. Market Share (2/2): Toll is the clear #1 U.S. luxury builder. Its average backlog price is $1,174,400, up from $1,161,000, and the price premium has held while Q3 FY2026 net signed contract value rose 5% to $2.52B [1]. Pipeline (0/2): Selling communities grew to 471 from 420. That is geographic expansion of the existing product, not a next-generation product roadmap [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): Homebuilders report no meaningful R&D spending.

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (2/4): The mission is to build luxury homes and communities that exceed customers' expectations through design, craftsmanship, and service. It clearly states what Toll does and for whom, but it describes a product promise, not a larger purpose [4]. Community Impact (0/2): Toll published its first ESG report in 2021 and discusses energy-efficient building, but our searches found no foundation or community program with dollar figures [6][7]. Employee Retention (2/2): Forbes ranked Toll the #1 Best Midsize Employer in 2022, 2025, and 2026. The new CEO is a 22-year internal hire who started in the company's executive training program, which points to strong internal leadership development [2][3]. Insider Buying (0/2): Insider activity over the past 12 months has been net selling, including director sales near $148 per share. We found no open-market purchases by executives [5].

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Scored mechanically as a Growth holding (sleeve forced by portfolios.json): 8.71 of 10 weighted points, which rounds to 9. D/E of 34.1% (1.00), Forward P/E of 10.6 (1.00), and Forward PEG of 0.90 (1.00, double weight) all meet target [5]. ROE of 14.4% (0.96, double weight) and the 5-year revenue CAGR of 9.2%, from $7.08B in FY2020 to $10.97B in FY2025 (0.95, double weight), sit just below target [5]. TTM revenue growth is the weak spot at -9.7% YoY (0.34), as Q3 FY2026 deliveries fell to 2,662 from 2,959. Profit margin is 11.1% (0.56) because adjusted gross margin fell to 25.6% from 27.5% [1]. Liquidity is about $144M per day, far above the floor.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): Toll's business is buying land, getting entitlements, and building homes with subcontractor crews. AI cannot replace any of these physical, locally regulated activities, and we found no analyst commentary describing AI as a substitution threat to luxury homebuilding [1][5]. The remaining risk is indirect: AI-driven white-collar job losses could weaken demand among affluent buyers. AI Opportunity (0/1): Toll reports no AI-derived revenue and has disclosed no AI products [3].

infinite_game.summary: Through a Sinek lens, Toll Brothers is a disciplined, durable builder that has lasted nearly 60 years and several housing cycles. Its strongest infinite-game trait is a high-trust culture that develops its own leaders. Its purpose is still product-centric luxury delivery, not a cause people would sacrifice for. Its capital allocation leans toward finite levers: buybacks were raised to $700M in FY2026 while deliveries are falling about 7%.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (1/3): The mission to 'exceed customers' expectations' with luxury homes is a service promise, not a vision of a future world. It is interchangeable with other premium builders and does not visibly guide strategy beyond product positioning [4].

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Management kept investing in land and grew selling communities about 12% YoY to 471 during a softening luxury market. It also protected price rather than chasing volume with heavy incentives [1]. However, raising FY2026 buybacks from $650M to $700M while revenue declines is a finite, per-share-optimizing choice [1].

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (2/2): Forbes named Toll the #1 Best Midsize Employer three times (2022, 2025, 2026). The 2026 CEO handoff went to Karl Mistry, a 22-year veteran who rose from assistant project manager. Yearley called this proof of a culture of 'cultivating and teaching the next generation of leadership' [2][3].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Toll has adapted incrementally, adding urban high-rise, active-adult, and build-to-rent apartment businesses and spreading from the Northeast to 24 states [4]. It has never reinvented its core business model.

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Management talks about competitors mainly in terms of pricing and share, such as the 'luxury premium' and spec-home competition. We found no evidence that Toll frames rivals as teachers that push it to improve [1][3].

investment_thesis: Toll Brothers is the dominant U.S. luxury homebuilder and trades at about 10.6x forward earnings and a 0.90 PEG. Its balance sheet is conservative at 34% D/E [5]. Demand is holding up: Q3 FY2026 net signed contract value rose 5% to $2.52B, and the average backlog price climbed to $1.17M, which shows the affluent buyer is still active [1]. Selling communities grew to 471 from 420, setting up volume growth in FY2027 [1]. Meanwhile $700M of FY2026 buybacks, about 5% of the market cap, supports per-share value [1].
thesis_continued: The bear case is cyclical compression. Q3 revenue fell 9.7% and EPS fell 20.4% to $2.97. FY2026 deliveries are guided down to 10,500-10,600 from 11,292, and adjusted gross margin has slipped about 190 bps to 25.6% [1]. Backlog value of $6.24B is below last year's $6.38B, so FY2027 revenue depends on spring selling and mortgage rates [1]. A new CEO only seven months into the job adds execution risk if the luxury market weakens further.
key_catalysts: Q4 FY2026 results in early December: guidance calls for $3.43-3.57B home sales revenue and a 26.1% full-year adjusted gross margin; beating it would confirm the margin trough
Community count up about 12% YoY to 471 selling communities, which should turn into FY2027 delivery growth if absorption pace holds
Falling mortgage rates would widen the buyer pool for $1M+ homes, many of which are bought partly with cash and so are less rate-sensitive
key_risks: Gross margin erosion: adjusted home sales gross margin fell to 25.6% from 27.5% YoY, and more incentives on spec homes could push it lower
Backlog value of $6.24B is down 2% YoY and homes in backlog are down 3%, which limits FY2027 revenue visibility
Wealth-effect sensitivity: a stock market correction would hit Toll's affluent buyer base directly and could stall contract growth
